original:
Use case: stylized-concept.
Create ONE isolated environment sprite for Emergency Shift, a fictional 2D overhead hospital horror video game: a small anonymous bloodied remnant of muscle and broken human bone, caught in torn medical clothing. This is ONE compact irregular fragment, not an entire person, not a torso portrait, not a sprite sheet.
Projection: strict orthographic view directly from above, camera 90 degrees downward. True transparent RGBA background. No ground, floor, surrounding glow, vignette, drop shadow, border, caption or watermark. Leave wide transparent margins.
Subject construction: a low, flattened asymmetric mass of dull grey-pink torn muscle, with two or three short curved ivory rib fragments still embedded in the same tissue. One rib fragment is longer and recognizable, another has a visibly irregular broken end, with a few small chips close to that fracture. Keep these related bones anatomically coherent, not a decorative collection of random bones or spikes. No skull, head, face, hands, feet, intact limb or complete body. Simple broad dark burgundy blood patches with a few slightly fresher red edges. Avoid intricate internal organs or anatomical micro-detail.
Medical identity: a partly attached ragged patch of faded teal scrub fabric and a smaller dirty ivory coat flap, a simple visible pocket-edge seam. Cloth is dragged and caught under one side, not neatly draped, folded in symmetry or centered on the meat. Blood soaks locally into the fabric; other areas retain recognizable hospital-clothing colors.
Art direction: restrained painted 2D game artwork, non-pixel, matte, coherent anatomical shapes, subtle surface variation, soft short shading limited to the fragment. NO photorealism, shiny studio 3D, heavy cartoon outlines, coarse polygon mosaic, or excessive noisy brush marks. Preserve readable separated bone, flesh and cloth masses at only 70–100 screen pixels across. Use a small number of clear muscle planes and a few meaningful fabric folds; no microscopic fibers, tiny veins or repeated uniform scratches.
The specific history of this piece is one crushed edge, a surviving curved bone, and cloth snagged to one side. Natural uneven contour, local damage, no perfect symmetry. One example only.

Use case: precise-object-edit.
Input image is the style and material reference for an Emergency Shift 2D hospital horror environment sprite. Create ONE DIFFERENT fragment in the same family, replacing the reference composition while retaining its muted flesh, ivory bone, dark blood and worn medical cloth appearance. Do not simply rotate or recolor the reference.
Strict direct overhead orthographic view, low flattened fragment lying in the ground plane. True transparent RGBA background, preserve transparency. No floor, vignette, cast shadow, outer glow, labels, border or watermark.
Anonymous fictional adult remains: muscle, related broken bone fragments and torn hospital clothing, no face, skull, head, hand, foot, whole limb or intact person. Painted 2D texture with readable large forms, not a photorealistic photograph or glossy studio model. Simplify tiny textures relative to the reference, keep a few clear flesh planes and fabric folds. No excessive fine anatomical detail. Readable at 70–120 screen pixels.
Natural irregularity must be specific: fragments are physically related, breaks uneven and cloth caught to one side, never bone spikes arranged as decoration, perfectly repeated shapes, centered packing or symmetrical blood stains.
Subject: a larger, broad crescent of flattened torn muscle with three short connected rib arcs emerging from one side. One rib remains a recognizable curve, a second is shorter and broken near its base, the third partly covered by muscle. Dull pink-grey fleshy planes and dark maroon blood with limited fresh wet spots. A small torn ivory lab-coat hem with one displaced button caught beneath the lower edge, very little teal cloth. Change silhouette and bone directions substantially from reference; do not recreate the same rectangular two-bone slab. Generous transparent margins.
